summary: Defines a vendor-specific suboption for the DHCP relay agent information option. It lets a relay agent add vendor-specific information to the DHCP messages it forwards, as set up by its administrator. It is a standards-track memo.

eli5.summary: A helper passing notes between you and the office can write an extra private note on each one. This memo gives that helper a place to put notes only certain companies understand.

questions: what is the dhcp vendor-specific suboption
what is an enterprise number in dhcp
how does a dhcp relay add vendor data
subtitle: A slot in the DHCP relay agent option where relays can attach vendor-defined data for the server.

tldr.problem: Existing relay agent suboptions (Remote-ID and Circuit-ID) usually carry values tied to the physical network, so administrators had no standard place to attach other vendor- or provider-specific data to relayed DHCP messages.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines suboption code 9 of the relay agent information option. It holds one or more blocks, each made of a vendor's IANA Enterprise Number, a data length and opaque vendor-defined bytes.
tldr.outcome: A configured relay can pass vendor-defined data to a DHCP server, which may use it when choosing addresses and configuration. The RFC sets no rules on what the data means.

today: RFC 4243 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2005. No RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Vendor-Specific Suboption
sections.content:
DHCP (RFC 2131) hands out IP addresses and configuration to IPv4 clients. A relay agent is a process in the network infrastructure that receives broadcast messages from clients and forwards them to DHCP servers as unicast messages. In environments such as DOCSIS data-over-cable and xDSL, it has proven useful for the relay to add information to the message first, using the relay agent information option from RFC 3046.

Servers that recognize that option echo it back in their replies. The information can help an edge device return replies to clients, and the server can also use it when deciding which addresses and parameters a client should get.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle can stick a note on each message before passing it on. The server reads the note to decide how to treat you.

sections.title: The Gap in Remote-ID and Circuit-ID
sections.content:
It is often desirable to tie vendor- or provider-specific information to a client's DHCP messages. RFC 3046 already defines the Remote-ID and Circuit-ID suboptions for carrying such information. Their values, however, are usually based on some network resource: the IP address of a network access device, an ATM Virtual Circuit identifier, or a DOCSIS cable-modem identifier.

That makes those values dependent on the physical network configuration. The Vendor-Specific suboption lets administrators associate other useful data with relayed DHCP messages.
sections.eli5: The old note slots only say where you plugged in. This new slot lets the helper write down anything else a company finds useful.

sections.title: The Suboption Format
sections.content:
The suboption looks like the Vendor-Identifying, Vendor-Specific Option from RFC 3925. Its Code is 9. The one-byte Length field gives the length of the data carried in the suboption, in bytes, including the first Enterprise Number. The minimum length is 4 bytes.

After that come one or more blocks. Each has an Enterprise Number, a four-byte integer in network byte order that is the vendor's number as registered with IANA, then a DataLen field giving the length of the data for that number, then the Suboption Data, an opaque sequence of bytes.

A relay may put data for more than one vendor's Enterprise Number into a single instance of the suboption. The RFC sets no requirements on the data itself, and encourages vendors who use the suboption to document their usage so that interoperability is possible.
sections.eli5: Each note has a company's ID number, a length, and then secret contents only that company understands. One note can hold bits for several companies.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A relay agent MAY be configured to include Vendor-Specific suboptions if it includes a relay agent information option in the DHCP messages it relays. How the suboptions' types and data are assigned and configured is outside the scope of the memo. Implementors are encouraged to let administrators configure what data goes in the suboption, and to document what the relay can do.

For the server, the suboption is extra input. A server that is configured to support it may use the information, together with other relay agent option data and other client options, to assign an IP address and/or other configuration parameters. There is no special additional processing for this suboption.
sections.eli5: The helper only adds the note if its boss told it to. The server may read the note when deciding what to give you, but it does not have to do anything special.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The relay agent option depends on a trusted relationship between relay and server, as described in section 5 of RFC 3046. Fraudulent relay agent option data could lead to theft of service or to exhaustion of limited resources such as IP addresses by unauthorized clients. A host that tampered with another host's relay data could deny service to it or lead the server to assign it inappropriate configuration.

A perimeter defense can block these options unless the relay is trusted, but the RFC says that a deeper defense using the Authentication Suboption (RFC 4030) SHOULD be deployed as well. Message authentication for intradomain DHCP is defined in RFC 3118.

Depending on what is put in it, the suboption may identify a specific host or user. In practice, DHCP messages are usually confined to the internal service-provider network, but if they travel outside it or the values become visible to other users, privacy concerns may arise for the access or service provider.
sections.eli5: If someone could forge the helper's notes, they might trick the server into giving them things. So the helper should be trusted, and the notes should not reveal private details to outsiders.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned suboption number 9 for the Vendor-Specific Information Suboption from the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option suboption number space. Vendors identify themselves inside the suboption using their Enterprise Number from the IANA Private Enterprise Numbers registry.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper reserved slot number 9 for this kind of note, so nobody else uses it for something different.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the suboption data in bytes, including the first Enterprise Number; minimum 4.

fields.name: Enterprise Number1 (first part)
fields.desc: Start of the first vendor's four-byte Enterprise Number, in network byte order.

fields.name: Enterprise Number1 (rest)
fields.desc: Rest of the first Enterprise Number.

fields.name: DataLen1
fields.desc: Length of the data for the first Enterprise Number.

fields.name: Suboption Data1
fields.desc: Opaque vendor-defined bytes; further Enterprise Number blocks may follow.
